blocks.text: V. The fifth, חנמל chanamal, Psal. LXXVIII, 47., is taken for the locust by R. Selomo and R. Chasan, whom Aben Ezra cites. But others more rightly hold that chanamal is something analogous to hail, so that, as usual, the two hemistichs of the same verse correspond (ἀντίστροφα [antistropha]). They read: And he destroyed בברד, with hail their vines, and their sycomores בחנמל, with Chanamal. So the Hebrew word for word. Accordingly Aben Ezra understands hailstones here. But Saadias and Kimchi understand what the Arabs call יאלצקיע, that is, hoarfrost ^{(6)}. Quite rightly. For so the ancient Greeks: Καὶ τὰς συκαμίνους αὐτῶν ἐν τῇ πάχνῃ [Kai tas sykaminous autōn en tē pachnē]. Hence the Vulgate translator: And their mulberry trees with hoarfrost. And the old Arabic Psalter in manuscript in my possession: وتوثهم بالصقيع [wa-tūthahum bi-l-ṣaqīʿ]. And the Ethiopic: ወበለሶሞን፡ በአስሐትያ፡; all in the same sense. Moreover, in the Midrash it is asserted that חנמל chanamal is said by metathesis for נחמל nachamal, because נח ומל nach vemal, it rests and cuts. Both of these suit hoarfrost very well. Hence Theophrastus, book 5, De causis, ch. 19, comparing snow with hoarfrost, says: Ἡ μὲν οὐκ ἐπιμένει, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποτήκεται ἀπὸ τῶν [col. 445] κλημάτων, καὶ τῶν βλαστῶν· ἡ δὲ πάχνη [Hē men ouk epimenei, all᾽ apotēketai apo tōn klēmatōn, kai tōn blastōn; hē de pachnē] (ἐπιμένουσα [epimenousa], for this must be supplied for the opposition to hold) ταῦτ᾽ ἀποκαίει [taut᾽ apokaiei], the former does not stay long, but melts and slips off the shoots and buds; but hoarfrost (staying long) burns them. And below: Τμητικοτέρα δοκεῖ ἡ πάχνη τῆς χίονος εἶναι [Tmētikotera dokei hē pachnē tēs chionos einai], Hoarfrost seems to have a greater power [III, 256] of cutting than snow. Pliny too writes that hoarfrost persidere [settles in], that is, stays settled long. The words are in book 17, ch. 24: Hoarfrost is more destructive by nature, because once fallen it stays settled. It is therefore very consistent with the truth that the word חנמל signifies hoarfrost rather than the locust. Ἐρυσίβη [erysibē], blight, is something else. Yet in the Greek Scholiast on the Psalms: ἐρυσίβη ἐςὶ κατὰ τὸν Ἡρωδιανὸν τὸ ἐπικάθιζον τοῖς καρποῖς παχνῶδες, καὶ διαφθεῖρον αὐτοὺς [erysibē esti kata ton Hērōdianon to epikathizon tois karpois pachnōdes, kai diaphtheiron autous], blight, according to Herodian, is that frost-like thing which settles on the fruits and spoils them ^{(7)}.

VI. The sixth name of the locust, חסיל chasil, is formed from the verb חסל chasal, which means to consume and is properly said of the locust. So in the Hebrew text, Deut. XXVIII, 38.: You shall cast much seed into the field and gather little, כי יחסלנו הארבה, for the locust shall consume it. And in the Chaldee of Onkelos: ארי יחסליניה גובא. And Nahum III, 16., in Jonathan: יחסלונך כגובא, They shall consume you like the locust. Hence, with the meaning somewhat altered, חסל also occurs frequently in the sense of finishing and completing, as if to consummate were nearly the same as to consume ^{(8)}.

[III, 257] VII. Where the seventh, חרגל chargol, comes from, the Hebrews are wholly ignorant. But in Arabic حرجل [ḥarjala] chargala means to be long, or to move and stretch out in a long line. Hence حرجل [ḥarjal] chargal, or حرجلة [ḥurjula] chorgola, in Alcamus, الجماعة من الخيل والقطعة مي الجراد [al-jamāʿa min al-khayl wa-l-qiṭʿa my al-jarād]: of horses it means a column; and of locusts, a swarm. Cadamustus, Navigations, ch. 13, writes that such a swarm sometimes extends over twelve miles. And although in Europe they extend less far, yet even there immense columns of locusts are sometimes seen. Aldrovandi, book 4, On insects, p. 423: They write that in the year 1475 a huge mass of locusts coming from Hungary, Moravia and Silesia roamed over the Sieradz and Łęczyca region and Masovia, etc., with swarms continuous for a mile and a half in breadth and as much again in length, that is, for three miles. Surius, at the year 1541, on the locusts around Poland: These flew forth in such a multitude that they covered two miles in length and breadth a cubit deep, so that by their density they shut out even the brightness of the sun from that whole tract of land. So it is not without reason that these columns of locusts take their name from a long line. Yet Moses does not use חרגל chargol for a swarm of locusts, but for a particular kind of locust. So too in the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath, fol. 67, in the Mishnah: יוצאין בביצת החרגל ובשן של שועל ובמסמר מן הצלוב משום רפואה, They go out (lawfully on the Sabbath day) with the egg of the chargol, and with the tooth of a fox, and with a nail from a gallows, for the sake of healing (hung on the body); and there the Gemara says that the egg of the chargol was used לשיחלא. And the Gloss says that שיחלא is כאבה און והרלי באזן, pain of the ear, or a disease in the ear ^{(9)}.
